Charger
CHAR-jer
n.
From charge in the older sense of to load—a charger is a vessel that is loaded, a large dish or platter. Old French chargier, to load, from Late Latin carricare. The war-horse sense is a later and separate development of the same verb, and does not appear in the KJV.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV a charger is a large serving dish—a platter—and never a horse or a battery. The word appears first in the tabernacle offerings, where each tribal prince brings one silver charger, the weight thereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, filled with fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering (Num 7:13). Twelve chargers, one per tribe, all identical: the charger is an instrument of ordered, weighed, covenant worship. Ezra records chargers returned among the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off, holy things counted back into their proper use. The word's other appearance is the most infamous in Scripture. Herodias instructs her daughter, and the girl asks Herod, Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger (Matt 14:8); Mark records the request with the same word, in a charger the head of John the Baptist (Mark 6:25). The horror is exact and deliberate: the vessel made for holy offering is used to serve up a prophet's head at a birthday feast. Scripture sets the two uses side by side without comment—the charger that carries fine flour to God, and the charger that carries a murdered man to a dancing girl—and lets the reader feel what a serving dish can be made to do.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives CHARGER first as a large dish or platter, and secondarily as a horse used for attack—the platter being the sense the KJV uses throughout.

expand to see more

CHARGER, n. — A large dish or platter. His offering was one silver charger (Num 7:13).

CHARGER, n. — A horse for attack or battle; a war horse. [This later sense is not the KJV usage.]

Key Scripture

Numbers 7:13 — "And his offering was one silver charger, the weight thereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary; both of them were full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering:"

Matthew 14:8 — "And she, being before instructed of her mother, said, Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger."

Mark 6:25 — "And she came in straightway with haste unto the king, and asked, saying, I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist."

Modern Corruption

Charger is corrupted mostly by simple drift: the modern reader hears a phone cable or a war-horse, and so misses that the vessel carrying John the Baptist's head is the same kind of vessel that carried fine flour to the altar.

expand to see more

The chief modern corruption of charger is not ideological but electrical. A reader raised on device cables meets Matthew 14:8 and either pictures nothing or pictures a horse, and either way the scene loses its point. The KJV word is a platter, and the platter is the connection: the same class of serving vessel that appears twelve times over in Numbers 7 loaded with fine flour for God turns up in a Galilean palace loaded with a prophet's head. Herod's feast is a black parody of the tabernacle offering, and the vocabulary is what carries the parody.

There is a further, milder corruption in the reverse direction: readers who do know the war-horse sense import it and imagine something martial in Numbers 7. Keep the order Webster keeps—platter first, horse as a later and separate development. Where a study Bible modernizes to platter, nothing doctrinal is lost; what is lost is the link between the two scenes, which the single KJV word preserves.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qe‘arah, a dish or platter of the sanctuary service; Greek pinax, a board, plank, or flat dish—the platter of Herod's feast.

expand to see more

Hebrew qe‘arah (H7086) — a dish or charger, used of the silver platters of the tribal offerings and of the tabernacle vessels (Exod 25:29; Num 7:13-85).

Greek pinax (G4094) — a board or plank, hence a flat dish or platter; used only of the charger bearing John's head and of the dish at the Pharisee's table (Matt 14:8, 11; Mark 6:25, 28; Luke 11:39).

Usage

"KJV sense is the platter: one silver charger, weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary."

"Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger—a worship vessel turned to a birthday atrocity."

"The war-horse meaning is later English and never the KJV's; Webster lists the dish first for that reason."
